1373.title: Three words for soul
1373.hook: nefesh, ruach and neshamah, all tied to breath and wind
1373.howItsDone: In the morning service Jews say Elohai neshamah, a blessing that thanks God for the pure soul placed within; teachers in the midrash and in Jewish mysticism speak of nefesh, ruach and neshamah as layers of the soul.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ch-Y-H: chai and chayim, and a law read as live by them, not die by them. Your line was l'chaim. Today, what the Torah says makes a body alive at all.

Before the coffee, before the phone, there's a short prayer in the morning service that speaks about the soul; you met it in year two. It runs something like this: my God, the soul you placed in me is pure. You created it, you formed it, you breathed it into me, and you keep it inside me. One verb jumps out. Breathed. Not built, not installed. The prayer leans on a scene at the start of Genesis, where God bends over a figure of earth and breathes. And Hebrew has more than one word for what English calls a soul. Today, three of them, and one verse where a breath passes between two.
screen: `A MORNING PRAYER.` → `YOU BREATHED IT INTO ME.` → `MORE THAN ONE WORD FOR SOUL.`

segments.voice: Three words. Take them one at a time, then together. First, nefesh. In the creation story the animals are called nefesh chayah, living creatures, and so, a chapter later, is the first human. Nefesh is the whole living being: the self that gets hungry, tired and scared. Second, ruach. In the second verse of Genesis, the King James says "the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters." The Hebrew under Spirit is ruach. After the flood, when "God made a wind to pass over the earth," that wind is ruach too. Translators reach for spirit in one place and wind in another; the Hebrew holds both at once. Third, neshamah, breath, the word the morning prayer uses. Now put them together, in Genesis chapter two: "and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." Breath of life: nishmat chayim, the neshamah. Living soul: nefesh chayah. Two of the three words share one sentence, and the thing between them is a breath. Later teachers, in the midrash and among the mystics, read these words as different sides or layers of the soul. Some readers keep it plainer. In this verse, a soul begins as something breathed in. You can't see it, but you can hear it, and you're doing it right now.
screen: `NEFESH: A WHOLE LIVING BEING.` · `RUACH: WIND, BREATH, SPIRIT.` · `NESHAMAH: THE BREATH OF LIFE.` · `ONE VERSE HOLDS TWO OF THEM.` · then, large: `נֶפֶשׁ · רוּחַ · נְשָׁמָה`

segments.voice: Breathe in slowly through your nose, all the way down, and let it out; then again, noticing the air arrive cool at the nostrils, the place the verse puts it. On the third breath out, let the word neshamah ride the breath silently, then stop counting and let the breath come on its own. If you pray, you can say the morning prayer's thought in your own way: the soul you placed in me is pure.
Three words for soul. Nefesh, a living being. Ruach, wind and spirit. Neshamah, breath. Today's word.
Your line: soul is breath. You're carrying it in and out right now. Three words, one breath.

1374.title: A-D-M
1374.hook: adam, adamah (earth), adom (red): the human is earthy
1374.howItsDone: Jews read the creation of adam from the adamah in Genesis, and the Mishnah in tractate Sanhedrin teaches from it that humans share one ancestry, so that no one may claim a greater lineage than another.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three words for soul: nefesh, ruach, neshamah, and a breath that made a figure alive. Your line was soul is breath. Today, the figure itself, and what it was made of.

A spade goes into a garden bed in spring and turns over a clump of earth: dark, damp, smelling of rain, a worm sliding out of sight. In Hebrew, that clump is adamah. Now look at the person holding the spade. In Hebrew, that's adam. Same three letters, alef, dalet, mem, with one small sound added for the ground. The gardener and the garden share a root. The Torah builds its first human out of the very word for soil, and then keeps playing with the sound.
screen: `A CLUMP OF EARTH: ADAMAH.` → `THE ONE HOLDING IT: ADAM.` → `THE SAME THREE LETTERS.`

segments.voice: A-D-M. Alef, dalet, mem. Turn it four ways. First, adamah, the ground. In Genesis chapter two, God forms the human "of the dust of the ground." Ground there is adamah. Second, the human: ha-adam. The story names its creature after its material, and some readers bring the pun into English as earthling. The next chapter says it out loud: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." Third, adom, red. Further on in Genesis, Esau comes in from the field, faint with hunger, and begs his brother for the red stew on the fire. Then the text adds: "therefore was his name called Edom." Red, Edom: the Torah makes that pun itself. Some readers go one step further and hear red in adam too, the reddish color of clay. Fourth, what the rabbis did with one clay. The Mishnah, in tractate Sanhedrin, asks why the human was created as a single person. One answer it gives: for the sake of peace, so that no one could say to another, my ancestor was greater than yours. Everyone traces back to one figure, and that figure to a handful of ground. Nobody's dust is finer than anyone else's. Not the king's, not yours, not anyone's.
screen: `ADAMAH: THE GROUND.` · `ADAM: NAMED FOR ITS MATERIAL.` · `ADOM: RED, LIKE EDOM'S STEW.` · `ONE CLAY, SO NO ONE OUTRANKS.` · then, large: `אָדָם · אֲדָמָה`

segments.voice: If there's soil nearby, a garden or a plant pot on the sill, put your fingers into it; if not, a stone, a wooden table or the floor under your feet will do. Feel the texture, cool or warm, gritty or smooth, and say the two words one after the other: adamah, adam, ground, human. If you pray, you can give thanks for being made of the earth.
A-D-M. Alef, dalet, mem: adamah, the ground; adam, the human made from it; and adom, red, the color of the clay and Edom's stew. Today's word.
Your line: human from earth. Same ground, so nobody's ancestor outranks anybody's. See you back here tomorrow.

1375.title: Sh-M-R
1375.hook: shamar: guard, keep, observe, as in keeping Shabbat
1375.howItsDone: Jews who observe the Sabbath are called shomer Shabbat, Sabbath keepers; the priestly blessing, which opens 'the LORD bless thee, and keep thee', is said in synagogue and by parents over children on Friday night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, A-D-M: adamah, the ground, and adam, the human made from it. Your line was human from earth. Today, the job that earth creature was given in Eden.

"Am I my brother's keeper?" It's a dodge. God has just asked Cain where his brother Abel is, and Cain, who knows exactly where Abel is lying, answers with a shrug turned into a question. In the King James it runs: "I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?" People still quote that line when they mean not my problem. But listen to the noun he picks. Keeper. In Hebrew, shomer: the one who guards, the one who keeps watch. Cain reaches for that word only to push it away. Today's root is the word he wouldn't take on.
screen: `WHERE IS ABEL?` → `AM I MY BROTHER'S KEEPER?` → `SHOMER: THE ONE WHO GUARDS.`

segments.voice: Sh-M-R. Shin, mem, resh. Guard, keep, watch, observe: English needs several words for one Hebrew root. Turn it four ways. First, the garden. God puts the human in Eden "to dress it and to keep it." Keep is shamar. The job handed over in Eden is guarding something that isn't theirs. Hold on to dress it, too; tomorrow's root is hiding there. Second, Cain. Two chapters later, the same job comes back as a refusal. The garden had a keeper; Cain won't be one for his own brother. God doesn't argue the point. The next words are about Abel's blood, crying out from the ground. The story answers the question. Third, God as keeper. The priestly blessing opens: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee." And a psalm promises, "he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep." The role Cain wouldn't touch, God takes on, without a night off. Fourth, keeping a day. When Deuteronomy repeats the Ten Commandments, the Sabbath line opens with shamor, keep, and a Jew who observes Shabbat is called shomer Shabbat, a Sabbath keeper. Put the four together and keeping looks less like storing something in a drawer and more like a watchman on a city wall at night. Whatever you keep, you also have to watch.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've said you'd do, the smallest one that's slipping: call your mother back, return the borrowed book, finish what you told a coworker you'd finish. Picture the exact moment you'll keep it, where you'll be and the first words you'll say, and guard that moment the way a watchman guards a gate. If you pray, you can ask for help keeping it.

Your line: keep and guard. Keeping, in this root, means watching over. That's today, done.

1376.title: A-V-D
1376.hook: avodah means both work and worship
1376.howItsDone: Jews call prayer avodah she-ba-lev, the service of the heart, after the rabbis' reading of Deuteronomy 11:13; on Yom Kippur the synagogue recalls the Temple's service in a section of prayers called the Avodah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sh-M-R: shamar, to guard, the job in Eden and the word Cain refused. Your line was keep and guard. Today, the other half of that garden job.

Moses stands in front of Pharaoh with a message he will carry again and again: "Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness." Serve. A strange word to bring to a king who already has the Hebrews building his store cities. They're already serving every day: mud, straw, brick, field. Moses isn't asking for them to stop serving. He's asking for them to serve someone else. In Hebrew, the brickwork and the worship use the same root.
screen: `LET MY PEOPLE GO.` → `THAT THEY MAY SERVE ME.` → `BRICKWORK AND WORSHIP: ONE ROOT.`

segments.voice: A-V-D. Ayin, vet, dalet. Avodah: work, labor, service, worship. Turn it four ways. First, back to yesterday's garden: "to dress it and to keep it." Keep was shamar. Dress is from this root: to work the soil, to till it. Before any altar or temple, avodah in the Eden story means digging. Second, Egypt. Early in Exodus comes a hard line: "they made their lives bitter with hard bondage." Bondage there is avodah. The same root names the worst thing in the story. Third, the way out. Let my people go, that they may serve me: serve is this root again. The exodus doesn't move the people from work to nothing. It moves their avodah from Pharaoh to God. And in Pirkei Avot, Shimon the Righteous teaches that the world stands on three things: Torah, avodah and acts of lovingkindness. Avodah there means the service in the Temple. Fourth, after the Temple. The rabbis read Deuteronomy's call "to serve him with all your heart" and ask what kind of service happens in the heart. Their answer, in tractate Taanit: prayer. Digging, slavery, offerings, prayer: one root runs through all of them. So its question isn't whether you work. It's who and what the work is for.
screen: `TO DRESS IT: WORKING THE SOIL.` · `HARD BONDAGE IN EGYPT.` · `SERVE ME: THE SAME ROOT.` · `SERVICE OF THE HEART: PRAYER.` · then, large: `עֲבוֹדָה`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the next ordinary task waiting for you: a spreadsheet, a load of laundry, a shift, a diaper. Ask the root's question, who is this for, maybe a customer, a child, a tired coworker, a stranger you'll never meet, and let the task belong to them for a minute. If you pray, you can offer the work to God before you start.
A-V-D. Ayin, vet, dalet: avodah, the work of the soil, the bondage in Egypt, the Temple service, and prayer, the service of the heart. Today's word.
Your line: work is worship. The question is who the work is for. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1377.title: M-L-Ch
1377.howItsDone: Jews say the Shema morning and evening, which the Mishnah calls accepting the yoke of the kingdom of heaven, and the standard blessing names God melech ha-olam, king of the world; on Rosh Hashanah a section of the service, Malchuyot, is devoted to God's kingship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, A-V-D: avodah, the work of the soil, the bondage in Egypt, the service of the heart. Your line was work is worship. Today, the question behind every service: who's in charge?

The elders of Israel walk to Ramah, to the prophet Samuel, who is old now, and put a request in front of him: "now make us a king to judge us like all the nations." Like everyone else. A palace, a crown, someone to lead the army out. The text says plainly how Samuel took it: "But the thing displeased Samuel." He goes to pray about it, and the answer he gets cuts two ways. That answer, and the Hebrew word for king inside it, is where today begins.
screen: `THE ELDERS COME TO SAMUEL.` → `MAKE US A KING.` → `THE THING DISPLEASED SAMUEL.`

segments.voice: M-L-Ch. Mem, lamed, chaf. Melech, a king. Malchut, kingship, a kingdom. And the verb, to reign. Turn it four ways. First, the answer Samuel gets. God tells him to listen to the people, and then: "they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them." Reign is this root. A human throne is granted, but with a long warning about what kings take: sons, daughters, fields, harvests. Kingship in the Bible starts with that tension built in. Second, a song sung long before. On the far shore of the sea, after the crossing, Moses and the people sing, and the song ends: "The LORD shall reign for ever and ever." They have no king of their own yet, and they sing that. Third, the blessings. The standard blessing names God melech ha-olam, king of the world, so the word comes up over bread, over wine, over a new fruit. Fourth, a kingdom you accept. The Mishnah, in tractate Berakhot, asks why the Shema's first paragraph comes before the next. Its answer: so that a person first takes on the yoke of the kingdom of heaven, ol malchut shamayim, and only then the yoke of the commandments. Kingship, in that picture, isn't seized or imposed. It's accepted, by the one saying the words, morning and evening. Which leaves a plain question: who, or what, rules here?
screen: `THEY HAVE REJECTED ME.` · `THE LORD SHALL REIGN FOR EVER.` · `MELECH HA-OLAM: KING OF THE WORLD.` · `THE YOKE OF THE KINGDOM, ACCEPTED.` · then, large: `מֶלֶךְ · מַלְכוּת`

segments.voice: Look back over the last few hours and ask what's been sitting on the throne: your phone, a deadline, a worry, a grudge, someone's opinion of you. Name it plainly without scolding yourself, then ask what you'd want ruling instead, kindness, a promise, God, your own best judgment, and let that sit on the throne for the rest of this quiet. If you pray, you can say the Shema, the way the Mishnah describes taking on the kingdom.
M-L-Ch. Mem, lamed, chaf: melech, a king; malchut, kingship; the reign the elders asked for and the one sung at the sea. Today's word.
Your line: kingship. Something always sits on the throne; the root asks who put it there. Rest well.

1378.title: G-A-L
1378.hook: geulah, go'el: redeem, as a relative redeems family land
1378.howItsDone: Jews read the book of Ruth on Shavuot, and the weekday Amidah includes a blessing to God as go'el Yisrael, the redeemer of Israel; geulah, redemption, is a hope that runs through Jewish prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, M-L-Ch: melech and malchut, a king asked for and a kingdom accepted. Your line was kingship. Today, a word for what a family does when something is lost.

Midnight, on a threshing floor. The barley harvest is in, and a landowner named Boaz has fallen asleep beside the grain heap. He wakes with a start: someone is lying at his feet. "Who art thou?" A widow, Ruth, the foreigner who has been gleaning in his field. She doesn't ask for money. She asks him to spread his cloak over her, and gives her reason in a single phrase: "for thou art a near kinsman." That phrase, near kinsman, is one Hebrew word: go'el. Today's root.
screen: `MIDNIGHT ON THE THRESHING FLOOR.` → `WHO ART THOU?` → `FOR THOU ART A NEAR KINSMAN.`

segments.voice: G-A-L. Gimel, alef, lamed. Go'el, the one who redeems. Geulah, redemption. Turn it four ways. First, the law behind the word. In Leviticus, if a man falls into poverty and sells part of his land, "if any of his kin come to redeem it, then shall he redeem that which his brother sold." To redeem is to buy back. The go'el is the relative who steps in so the family doesn't lose its ground. Second, the gate. The morning after the threshing floor, Boaz sits at the town gate, because a relative closer than he is has the first right to redeem a field that belonged to Naomi's late husband. That man is ready to buy the field, until he learns Ruth comes with it. Then he backs away: "I cannot redeem it for myself." Boaz steps in, and the land and the family stay together. Third, God as go'el. In Egypt, before the plagues, God says to the enslaved people: "I will redeem you with a stretched out arm." God is cast as the near relative who comes to buy the family back. Fourth, the prayer. In the weekday Amidah, one blessing calls God go'el Yisrael, the redeemer of Israel, and geulah is something Jews still pray toward. So redemption in this root isn't vague. It looks like a relative walking to the gate and paying what it costs to bring someone home.
screen: `THE GO'EL BUYS BACK THE LAND.` · `A CLOSER KINSMAN SAYS NO.` · `I WILL REDEEM YOU.` · `GO'EL YISRAEL, IN THE AMIDAH.` · then, large: `גּוֹאֵל · גְּאֻלָּה`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that slipped from where it should be but could still be bought back: a friendship gone quiet after a sharp word, a promise half kept, your own garden gone to weeds. Ask what it would cost, a phone call, an apology, an hour, a bit of pride, and settle on the one step you'd take, the way Boaz walked to the gate. If you pray, you can ask for help with it.
screen: `WHAT WOULD IT COST TO BUY BACK?`

segments.voice: G-A-L. Gimel, alef, lamed: go'el, the near relative who buys back what was lost, and geulah, redemption. Today's word.

1379.title: N-Ch-M
1379.howItsDone: Visitors to a shiva house sit with the mourners, wait for them to speak first, and on leaving say ha-Makom yenachem, may the Place comfort you; the Shabbat after Tisha b'Av is called Shabbat Nachamu, after the opening of Isaiah 40, its prophetic reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, G-A-L: the go'el, who walks to the gate and buys back what was lost. Your line was redeem. Today, what family does when the loss can't be bought back.

A house with the mirrors covered. The front door is left unlocked so nobody has to ring. Inside, the mourners sit on low stools, and visitors come in quietly with trays of food and sit near them. By an old custom, the visitors don't start talking. They wait, sometimes a long while, until the mourner speaks first. Leaving, they say a set line in Hebrew, something like: may God, called here the Place, comfort you among the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem. The verb in that line, yenachem, comes from today's root.
screen: `A SHIVA HOUSE.` → `THE VISITORS WAIT.` → `MAY THE PLACE COMFORT YOU.`

segments.voice: N-Ch-M. Nun, chet, mem. Nechamah, comfort. Turn it four ways. First, the prophet. Isaiah chapter forty opens: "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God." In Hebrew, nachamu, nachamu: said twice, as if once weren't enough. That chapter is read on the Shabbat after Tisha b'Av, the day of mourning for the Temples, and that Shabbat takes its name from the first word: Shabbat Nachamu. Second, a baby's name. When Noah is born, his father Lamech explains the name: "This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands." The text ties the boy's name to comfort, after the curse on the ground that made work so hard. Third, Joseph. After Jacob dies, his brothers are afraid Joseph will finally pay them back for selling him. Instead, "he comforted them, and spake kindly unto them." More literally, he spoke to their heart: not a speech about what went wrong, but words aimed at the heart. Fourth, the shiva house, which you sat in earlier this year. Yenachem, may God comfort you. The visitors don't claim to do the comforting themselves. They sit, they wait, they bring food, and they hand the comfort back to the Place. A prophet's doubled cry, a baby's name, a brother's kind words, a quiet visit: one root.
screen: `NACHAMU: COMFORT YE, COMFORT YE.` · `NOAH: THIS SAME SHALL COMFORT US.` · `JOSEPH SPOKE TO THEIR HEART.` · `YENACHEM: MAY THE PLACE COMFORT YOU.` · then, large: `נַחֲמוּ נַחֲמוּ`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person carrying something heavy, a loss, an illness, a job gone, a quiet loneliness, and picture yourself sitting near them the way visitors sit at a shiva: not fixing, not explaining, just there. Think of a few words aimed at the heart, the way Joseph spoke to his brothers, and hold them until they feel right; if you pray, you can ask that they be comforted. And if the heavy thing is yours, and you're in danger or thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.
N-Ch-M. Nun, chet, mem: nechamah, comfort, from nachamu to yenachem. This week's roots ran soul, earth, keep, work, king, redeem, and comfort. Today's word.
Your line: comfort. Sometimes it's simply being there, with words aimed at the heart. Go gently.
